title: Noach: the cloak carried backward (Genesis 9:20–27)
hookLine: Noah drinks and falls; two sons cover him, walking backward

cards: Everyone has seen someone at their worst. A relative at a wedding who had too much. A coworker who cried in the bathroom.
A friend whose embarrassing video went around the group chat. In that moment you have a choice, and it happens fast. You can look.
You can take a picture. You can tell everyone. Or you can quietly help cover it up and walk away.
The Torah has a story about exactly that moment, and it happens to Noah, the whole-hearted man who just saved the world.

teach.b: After the flood, Noah becomes a farmer and plants a vineyard, the first vineyard in the Torah. He drinks the wine, gets drunk, and lies uncovered in his tent.
The hero of the flood, lying exposed, and the Torah doesn't hide it. One of his sons, Ham, sees his father like that, and goes out and tells his two brothers.
That's his whole act: he saw, and he told.

Then Shem and Japheth take a garment, lay it on both their shoulders, and walk in backward. The text slows down: they "went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father," their faces turned away, so they never saw.
It's an almost awkward picture: two grown men shuffling backward into a tent, holding a cloak between them, so they can help without looking. Rashi notices a small thing in the Hebrew.

The verb for took is singular: he took. That teaches, Rashi says, that Shem moved first, with extra eagerness, and Japheth joined him. When Noah wakes, he blesses Shem and Japheth, and curses Canaan, Ham's son.

That curse has a painful later history. Centuries after, some people twisted it, calling it the curse of Ham, to justify slavery. But the text curses Canaan, not Ham, and says nothing at all about skin or color.
That reading was a misuse, and it did real harm. The story's own lesson is simpler. The rabbis taught that shaming someone in public is like shedding their blood.
Noah's sons show the other way.
When someone falls, you can bring a cloak, and turn your face.

how: Jewish teachers read this passage alongside the Talmud's teaching that publicly shaming someone is like shedding blood, and use it to teach protecting others' dignity.

games.q: you're one of Noah's sons. your brother says he's just seen your father drunk and uncovered in his tent. what do you do?
o: take a cloak and walk in backward.
tell the rest of the family.
games.why: Shem and Japheth put a garment on their shoulders and walked in backward, faces turned away, so they never saw.

practice: Remember a time you saw someone embarrassed, or at their worst, and how you responded; then a time someone saw you like that, and covered for you, or didn't, and what that felt like.
Now picture yourself walking backward into that moment, holding a cloak, face turned away, giving someone back their dignity.

wordCard.voice: Noach. The portion of Noah, where two sons walk backward with a cloak to cover their father without looking.

carryVoice: Your line: walk backward with the cloak. Dignity, carried on two pairs of shoulders. Until tomorrow.
